transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you too. Um, well, I guess what finally brought me in is... I just feel like the part of me that used to reach out for people and take pleasure in things has gone very quiet. Like my work—I'm a social worker, mostly handling substance abuse cases, and I used to really feel energized by it. Or my hobbies. I used to do a lot of yoga, and I loved going to art galleries. 

Actually, there was this one gallery downtown that had the most beautiful watercolor exhibit a few weeks ago. The artist was from Oregon, I think? Or Washington. Somewhere out West. I went to Oregon once for a graduate seminar, and it rained the entire time, which makes sense for watercolors when you think about it. The water just bleeds into the paper so naturally when the air is damp like that. I bought a really nice umbrella on that trip, one of those ones with the wooden handles... 

But, um... what was I saying? Right, the galleries. I just don't care to go to them anymore. Even my journaling, which I used to do every night. It's all just... quiet. I’m mostly just moving through my daily obligations at this point, just going through the motions.
Have you ever felt this way for a period of two weeks or longer at any point in your life before now?

Two weeks... um, no, I don't think so. Not that I can remember. If I ever felt a little flat before, it was usually just for a day or two. Like around the holidays, you know? Thanksgiving can be so draining. My sister insists on hosting every single year, but her oven is practically an antique. Last year the turkey took an extra three hours, and we were all just sitting around her living room eating celery sticks. 

Celery is such a strange vegetable when you think about it. It’s basically just crunchy water. Unless you put peanut butter on it, I guess. My clients at the clinic actually love when I bring in snacks—the peanut butter crackers are always the very first thing to disappear from the basket in the waiting room. I usually buy them in bulk at Costco. Have you been to the new one they opened on the west side? The parking lot is an absolute nightmare, they designed the lanes completely wrong so everyone gets bottlenecked near the tire center... but anyway, yeah, I don't think I've ever felt this quiet for this long before.
Do you notice that these feelings of 'quietness' or low mood tend to follow a consistent pattern in relation to your menstrual cycle?

My menstrual cycle? Um, no, I haven't really noticed any pattern with that. I mean, my cycle has been a little all over the place lately anyway, which I guess is just part of getting older. Forty-nine is a weird age. You're not quite old, but you definitely aren't young anymore either. 

Speaking of getting older, my aunt just turned seventy last weekend, and we had this big surprise party for her at this Italian restaurant she loves. They make their own pasta from scratch right there in the window. You can actually stand outside on the sidewalk and watch them rolling out the dough. It takes so much upper body strength to do that all day. I tried making homemade pasta once during lockdown—everyone was baking sourdough, but I decided I was going to master ravioli. It was a complete disaster. The dough was way too sticky, and I ended up getting flour all over my cat. He's a black cat, so he looked like a little ghost running around the apartment for three days. I had to bribe him with tuna just to get him into the bathroom so I could wipe him down with a damp towel... 

But, um, what were you asking? Oh, right, my cycle. No, I don't think the quietness is connected to that. It just feels like it's there all the time now.
Could you tell me how long this 'quiet' feeling has been present—has it been going on for a few months, or has it been more like a couple of years?

Um, let me think. It hasn't been years, no. I'd say this whole change... just how I'm thinking, my work, how I connect with people... it's been going on for about eight months. Yeah, right around the time we took my older relative into our apartment. 

Which, honestly, has been a huge adjustment in itself. We had to completely rearrange the guest room to fit her hospital bed, and we ended up donating this beautiful antique writing desk that used to be in there. I found it at a flea market in upstate New York years ago. The guy selling it said it belonged to a local poet, but you know how those stories go—they probably just made it up to get an extra fifty bucks. Still, it had these little brass drawer pulls shaped like oak leaves. Oak trees are so fascinating, aren't they? The way their root systems communicate with each other underground... I watched a documentary about it on PBS one night when I couldn't sleep. The narrator had this incredibly soothing British accent. I think he's the same guy who does the voiceovers for those nature shows about the deep ocean. The ocean terrifies me, honestly. All that dark water, and those fish with the little glowing lights on their heads... 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, right. Eight months. Yeah, about eight months since she moved in.

Looking back further than just the last few years, have you ever experienced a period of at least two weeks where you felt this same persistent low mood, loss of interest, or inability to enjoy things?

Further back? Like, when I was younger? Um... no, honestly. I don't think I've ever had a two-week block where I felt like this in the past. Two weeks is actually a really long time to feel nothing. It's like a whole pay period at the clinic. 

Speaking of payroll, they just switched our software system again at work, and it has been an absolute nightmare. The HR director—she's this woman named Brenda who always wears these incredibly loud floral scarves—she sent out a forty-page PDF manual on how to log our hours. Forty pages! Who has time to read that? I ended up printing it out, and it jammed the copier on the second floor. That copier is always jamming anyway. I think someone spilled coffee in it back in 2019 and they just never properly cleaned the inside. Coffee stains are impossible to get out, especially on electronics. I spilled a latte on my laptop in grad school right before my final thesis was due. I cried for about three hours straight because I thought I lost all my client case studies... 

But that was just stress, you know? Not this... quietness. So, yeah, no. I've never had two weeks of this before now.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your appetite or your ability to sleep since you started feeling this way eight months ago?

Appetite or sleep... um, no, not really. I haven't noticed any big changes with either of those. I mean, I still eat my regular meals, and my sleep is about the same as it usually is. 

Sleep is such a funny thing, though, isn't it? Like, how we just power down for eight hours a day. I read an article recently about how dolphins sleep with one half of their brain awake at a time so they don't drown. Can you imagine? Just swimming around, half asleep, half awake. I wonder what that feels like. Probably like being in a really boring staff meeting right after lunch. We had one of those last Tuesday, actually. They brought in sandwiches from that deli down the street—the one with the neon sign that's always flickering. I got the turkey and swiss, but the bread was a little stale. I think they bake it the day before. Baking bread is an art, really. My grandmother used to bake the most amazing rye bread. The smell would fill the whole house... 

But anyway, yeah. My sleep and appetite are fine. No changes there.
Have you noticed any persistent feelings of fatigue or a significant decrease in your energy levels over these past eight months?

Fatigue? Um... no, I wouldn't say I've felt fatigued. My energy is pretty much normal, just... you know, the usual amount. 

Energy is a weird concept when you think about it. Like, where does it actually go? I was trying to explain this to one of my clients the other day—he’s this teenager who’s really into physics and comic books. He was telling me all about the laws of thermodynamics, how energy can't be created or destroyed, just transformed. It made me think about those old wind-up toys. My brother had this little tin robot when we were kids. You'd crank the key on its back, and it would march across the kitchen floor until the spring unwound. It made this awful grinding noise on the linoleum. Our kitchen floor was that horrible mustard yellow color that was so popular in the seventies. My mom hated it, but my dad refused to rip it up because he said it hid dirt well. He was always so practical like that. He used to keep a spreadsheet for everything, even his lawn care schedule...

But no, I'm not feeling extra tired or anything. My energy levels are fine.
Do you find yourself feeling overly critical of yourself, or feeling like you are a burden or a failure to others?

A burden? Or a failure? Um... no, not really. I don't feel overly critical of myself. I mean, I do my job and I know I'm good at it, so no. 

People are so quick to use words like 'failure' though, especially in my field. It always reminds me of those annual performance reviews we have to do every December. My supervisor, David—he's this guy who insists on using a red fountain pen for all the evaluation forms. Who even buys fountain pens anymore? He says it makes his signature look more authoritative, but the ink just bleeds right through the cheap paper they buy for the office. Once, he left it uncapped in his shirt pocket and it leaked everywhere. It was a crisp white button-down, too. He had to walk around the clinic the rest of the day with this massive red stain over his chest, looking like an extra in a slasher movie. I really can't stand horror movies, honestly. They rely way too much on cheap jump scares these days instead of actual psychological suspense. Hitchcock knew how to do it right. Rear Window is an absolute masterpiece. The way he uses the camera to make you feel like a voyeur, just watching the neighbors... 

But, um... what was the question? Oh, right, being a burden. No, I definitely don't feel like that.
You mentioned that you've lost interest in your hobbies and social interactions; are there any activities at all, even small ones, that you still find yourself enjoying?

Enjoying things? Um... honestly, no. And I think that's what finally brought me in here. I just feel like the part of me that used to reach for people, or take pleasure in things... my work, yoga, art galleries, even my journaling... it’s all just gone very quiet. 

Journaling used to be such a big deal for me. I’d buy these specific leather-bound notebooks from a little stationary shop downtown. The owner always had classical music playing. Usually Bach. Cellos have such a distinct sound, don't they? It vibrates right in your chest. My niece started playing the cello last year. She's only nine, so the instrument is practically bigger than she is, and they have to use this special anchor strap so it doesn't slip on their hardwood floors. Hardwood floors are an absolute nightmare to keep clean, especially in the winter with all the rock salt people track in from the sidewalks. You have to sweep constantly or it completely ruins the polyurethane finish. My sister spends half her weekend just sweeping... 

But anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, enjoying activities. Yeah, no. I don't really have that right now. I’m mostly just moving through obligations.

He had to walk around the clinic the rest of the day with this massive red stain over his chest, looking like an extra in a slasher movie. I really can't stand horror movies, honestly. They rely way too much on cheap jump scares these days instead of actual psychological suspense. Hitchcock knew how to do it right. Rear Window is an absolute masterpiece. The way he uses the camera to make you feel like a voyeur, just watching the neighbors... 

But, um... what was the question? Oh, right, being a burden. No, I definitely don't feel like that.

F34.1 (Dysthymia) remains a strong consideration given the duration and lack of full symptomatic criteria.

patient.answer:
Enjoying things? Um... honestly, no. And I think that's what finally brought me in here. I just feel like the part of me that used to reach for people, or take pleasure in things... my work, yoga, art galleries, even my journaling... it’s all just gone very quiet. 

Journaling used to be such a big deal for me. I’d buy these specific leather-bound notebooks from a little stationary shop downtown. The owner always had classical music playing. Usually Bach. Cellos have such a distinct sound, don't they? It vibrates right in your chest. My niece started playing the cello last year. She's only nine, so the instrument is practically bigger than she is, and they have to use this special anchor strap so it doesn't slip on their hardwood floors. Hardwood floors are an absolute nightmare to keep clean, especially in the winter with all the rock salt people track in from the sidewalks. You have to sweep constantly or it completely ruins the polyurethane finish. My sister spends half her weekend just sweeping... 

But anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, enjoying activities. Yeah, no. I don't really have that right now. I’m mostly just moving through obligations.
